topic.subject: general
topic.title: Sleep and the body
topic.scope: why we sleep, sleep needs of teenagers, screens before bed, sleep and memory, myths about catching up on sleep

nodes.name: Why we sleep and what sleep does
Growth hormone is released mostly in deep sleep
Sleep helps the immune system fight infection
Sleep before learning helps the brain take in new facts
The brain stays active during sleep
Sleep has cycles of light, deep and dream sleep
Teen body clock shifts later in puberty
Sleepiness in the morning in teens is biological, not laziness
Poor sleep lowers concentration and school performance
Bright screen light delays the sleep hormone melatonin
Content on screens keeps the mind alert
Switch screens off 30-60 minutes before bed
Fixed sleep and wake times help
Caffeine drinks late in the day disturb sleep
Weekend long sleep cannot fully repay weekday sleep debt
Sleep quality matters, not only hours

misconceptions.statement: Sleep is just the body switching off to rest, and nothing useful happens.
misconceptions.why: The sleeping person is still and unresponsive, so it looks like nothing is happening.
misconceptions.fix: During sleep the body repairs itself, releases hormones, fights germs and the brain organises memories.

probe.question: What useful work does your body do while you sleep?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, it just rests like a switched-off machine.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not happen

misconceptions.statement: The brain completely switches off when we sleep.
misconceptions.why: People are unaware of their surroundings, so students assume the brain stops.
misconceptions.fix: The brain stays very active in sleep, and in dream sleep it is nearly as active as when awake.

probe.question: Is the brain active during sleep?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it switches off until morning.

misconceptions.statement: Everyone of every age needs exactly 8 hours of sleep.
misconceptions.why: The '8 hours' rule is repeated everywhere, so students treat it as one number for all ages.
misconceptions.fix: Sleep needs depend on age. Children aged 6-12 need about 9-12 hours and teenagers about 8-10 hours, while adults need about 7-9 hours.

probe.question: A 7-year-old and a 40-year-old both sleep exactly 8 hours. Are both getting the right amount?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because everyone needs exactly 8 hours.

misconceptions.root_belief: One sleep duration fits all ages
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO or national health guidelines on sleep duration

misconceptions.statement: Teenagers sleep late only because they use phones and are not disciplined.
misconceptions.why: Students and adults blame the late bedtime on habits alone and ignore the body's own timing change.
misconceptions.fix: During puberty the body clock shifts later, so teens feel sleepy later at night. Phones can make it worse, but they are not the only cause.

probe.question: Why does a teenager often not feel sleepy until 11 pm or later?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they use phones and lack discipline, nothing else.

misconceptions.root_belief: Behaviour alone explains teen sleep timing

misconceptions.statement: Missing sleep only makes you feel tired and has no other effect on the body.
misconceptions.why: Students link sleep loss only with the feeling of tiredness.
misconceptions.fix: Too little sleep also lowers attention and memory, affects mood, weakens the body's defence against infection and can slow growth in children.

probe.question: A student sleeps 4 hours daily for a week. Apart from tiredness, what changes?

misconceptions.source_hint: school health textbook or public health sleep guidance

misconceptions.statement: The body clock works only on how tired we are, and light does not affect it.
misconceptions.why: Students think sleepiness comes only from effort and activity during the day.
misconceptions.fix: The body clock is set mainly by light. Bright light in the morning keeps it on time, and light at night delays it.

probe.question: Does sitting in a brightly lit room at night change when you feel sleepy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, sleepiness depends only on how much work you did.

misconceptions.statement: Watching TV or a phone in bed helps you relax and fall asleep faster.
misconceptions.why: Screens feel relaxing, so students assume they help sleep.
misconceptions.fix: Screen light delays melatonin, and exciting content keeps the mind alert, so screens before bed usually make it harder to fall asleep.

probe.question: Will watching videos in bed for an hour help you sleep sooner?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it relaxes you so you fall asleep faster.

misconceptions.source_hint: studies on adolescent bedtime screen use

misconceptions.statement: Sleeping very long on Sunday fully makes up for sleeping little all week.
misconceptions.why: Students think sleep is like a bank balance that can be repaid in one go.
misconceptions.fix: Weekend sleep gives some relief, but it cannot fully repay weekday sleep debt, and it can upset the body clock. Regular sleep is better.

probe.question: You slept 5 hours on weekdays and 12 hours on Sunday. Is the damage fully repaired?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the extra hours cancel the lost sleep completely.

misconceptions.root_belief: Lost sleep can be repaid fully later

misconceptions.statement: A cup of tea or cola at night does not affect sleep because it is a cold or sweet drink.
misconceptions.why: Students link caffeine only with hot coffee and ignore it in other drinks.
misconceptions.fix: Tea, cola and energy drinks contain caffeine, which keeps you alert for hours and can delay and disturb sleep if taken late.

probe.question: Does a cola at 9 pm affect sleep?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only hot coffee affects sleep.

misconceptions.source_hint: health guidance on caffeine in drinks

misconceptions.statement: Studying hard through the night before an exam is better than sleeping.
misconceptions.why: Students believe more hours of study always means more marks.
misconceptions.fix: Sleep helps the brain store what was studied and keeps attention sharp for the exam. Good sleep after studying helps more than extra hours awake.

probe.question: Is it better to stay up all night studying or sleep 8 hours before the exam?
probe.wrong_answer: Stay up, because more study time gives more marks.

misconceptions.root_belief: More waking study always beats sleep
misconceptions.source_hint: research on sleep and learning in students

misconceptions.statement: We dream throughout the night in the same way, and sleep is one single steady state.
misconceptions.why: Students picture sleep as one flat stretch with no stages.
misconceptions.fix: Sleep moves in cycles of light, deep and dream (REM) sleep, repeated several times each night, and the brain behaves differently in each.

probe.question: Is the brain doing the same thing in the first hour and the fourth hour of sleep?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sleep is the same all night.

misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT or standard biology sources on sleep stages

misconceptions.statement: Children grow taller during the day while awake and sleep has nothing to do with growth.
misconceptions.why: Students link growth only with food and exercise.
misconceptions.fix: Growth hormone is released mostly in deep sleep, so sleep helps children's growth along with food and activity.

probe.question: Does sleep help a child grow taller?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only food and exercise help growth.

misconceptions.root_belief: Growth depends only on food and exercise
